LAN, WAN and the Internet
A Local Area Network (LAN) connects devices in a home, building or local campus.
03
A local network
PCs, a printer and a local server
share local connectivity
Other networks
Across a Wide Area Network
(WAN)
or the Internet
Router /
gateway
Local services can keep working even when the Internet connection fails.
SOHO: Small Office / Home Office.
Often combines a router, switch
and Access Point (AP).
Enterprise / campus: more users and switches,
possibly across nearby buildings.

Local delivery or the default gateway
PC A uses 192.168.10.10/24. Here, /24 means mask 255.255.255.0.
08
PC A’s local subnet: 192.168.10.0/24
Destination 192.168.10.20
The first 24 bits match.
A sends locally to the destination’s MAC
address.
A router is unnecessary for this path.
Destination 192.168.20.20
The first 24 bits differ.
A sends to its default gateway’s MAC address.
The IP destination stays 192.168.20.20.
Gateway: 192.168.10.1. Assume only a connected subnet and a default route.
No more-specific routes apply in this example.
ARP finds the next hop’s MAC address
Address Resolution Protocol maps a local IPv4 address to a MAC address.
09
Broadcast request Receive reply Record and use MAC
Valid cached mapping? Use the cached MAC
No: cache miss
A asks: “Who has 192.168.10.20?”
Yes: cache hit
B replies. A records and uses B’s MAC.
For a remote IP destination, A resolves the gateway’s local IP address instead.

Across routed Ethernet hops, MAC addresses change. Without NAT, end-to-end IP addresses remain.
Example assumes no network address translation (NAT).
Ethernet links: media, speed and duplex
Modern switched Ethernet normally uses point-to-point, full-duplex links.
15
Concept
What to remember
Copper and fiber
Copper carries electrical signals. Fiber carries light.
Link speed
An agreed link rate is a capacity, not guaranteed application throughput.
Full duplex
Both ends can send simultaneously. Correct full
-duplex links have no collisions.
Legacy half duplex
Shared Ethernet used CSMA/CD for collisions. Full duplex does not.
Illustration: 100 Mb/s ÷ 8 = 12.5 MB/s before overhead and other bottlenecks.
CSMA/CD = Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection.
Mb/s = megabits per second. MB/s = megabytes per second.

Mini-lab: build and observe a two-PC LAN
Use two lab PCs or a network simulator. Keep the lab separate from a production network.
17
Build
Connect A and B to a switch.
Set A to 192.168.10.10/24.
Set B to 192.168.10.20/24.
Use the same VLAN. Leave the gateway blank for
this local-only lab.
Observe
On Windows, run ipconfig /all.
Run ping 192.168.10.20 from A.
Run arp -a before and after.
If the switch is managed, inspect its MAC
address table.
Predict first: Can A reach B without a router? Which address appears in A’s ARP cache?
Expected result: a local path can work without a gateway. Check host firewalls if ping fails.
Knowledge check
Write your answers before moving to the next slide.
18
01 A can print locally, but websites fail. Is the LAN necessarily down?
02 A is 192.168.10.10/24. B is 192.168.20.20. Whose MAC should A use?
03 Does a switch learn from the source MAC or destination MAC?
04 Will a broadcast in VLAN 10 normally reach endpoints in VLAN 20?
05 A can ping a remote IP, but a hostname fails. What should you investigate?
Answer key and explanations
Use the explanation, not just the short answer, to check your understanding.
19
01 No. Local printing demonstrates a working local path. Check the gateway, WAN or DNS.
02 The gateway’s MAC. The remote host is outside A’s /24. Keep the remote host’s destination IP.
03 The source MAC. The switch associates that source with the arrival port and VLAN.
04 No. VLANs bound Layer 2 broadcasts. Communication between VLANs needs routing.
05 Investigate name resolution. Check DNS settings and a name lookup, while considering other
causes.
